A1.notes.Q3: Course grades help me spot struggles, so moderate improvement is okay. Admissions data feels invasive; I'd need a large jump to justify it. Absalon activity data (page views) terrifies me—feels like surveillance—and requires no threshold ever. Sensitive info: disability status helps fairness and might be acceptable if we catch more kids in need.
A1.notes.Q4: I value explainability highly because students need to trust the system and we can guide them properly if they flag something wrong. Very low explainability is never acceptable for me.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness cannot come at the cost of missing students who actually need help, as that leaves them in crisis without support. I'd accept a small drop overall (up to ~3) if it means we stop unfairly ignoring marginalized groups.
A1.notes.Q6: Generic emails often get ignored or cause panic. A personalized message from me as an advisor, followed by a voluntary meeting to discuss specific options, builds the trust students need.
A1.notes.Q7: If we just send generic emails, too many people get spammy outreach while serious cases slip through if I don't flag them myself. A balance is safer than casting a wide net.

A2.notes.Q3: Credits + grades are standard admin data, so moderate improvement is enough for Q3.2. High-school GPA (Q3.3) adds bias risk; need large gain to justify. Online behavior (Absalon/Q3.4) is too intrusive personally—acceptable even without extra accuracy because it signals genuine struggle better than guessing.
A2.notes.Q4: I work with students daily; they need to trust the flag before meeting me. High explainability is essential for rapport. If a model says 'low,' I won't know how to talk about it, so no answer for very low.
A2.notes.Q5: As someone who sees struggling students often feel ignored if a group is under-served, I accept losing ~5% overall ID rate to ensure equity. We can't afford missing marginalized students due to systemic bias.
A2.notes.Q6: Students don't want long waiting periods if they are struggling. Once flagged, immediate contact is crucial for early intervention.
A2.notes.Q7: With a generic email (many students), noise increases and trust decreases—so balance it out. With personalized emails from an advisor, the cost of false positives is high; better to be fewer but precise.
A2.Q8.1: We need human-in-the-loop review before acting on any model flag, otherwise we risk automating inequality into student life plans.

A3.notes.Q3: Using Absalon data feels invasive without strict context, especially for non-performing students. Admissions data is useful but raises concerns about bias from high-school grades.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is essential for students to accept help; if I'm flagged without a clear reason, I might distrust the system and disengage from support.
A3.notes.Q5: We cannot afford false positives (unnecessary contact), but missing struggling students is also harmful. Prioritizing fairness in reducing unnecessary flags protects student dignity more.
A3.notes.Q6: Continuously flagging students creates stigma and anxiety, even if well-intentioned. A periodic check-in feels more supportive.
A3.notes.Q7: With personalized outreach, errors cost more; a false positive could deeply distress a student or damage their relationship with advisors.
A3.Q8.1: Students may hide struggles from the model because they fear it triggers unwanted surveillance rather than help.

S1.notes.Q3: Course credits are boring, but grades help me see if I'm struggling now. Admissions data seems irrelevant to my current study situation. But Absalon activity (page views) feels like being watched constantly; it's intrusive for daily work studies.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged so my advisor can explain it. 'The model says' feels insulting and shuts down conversation. Without a human explaining the specific academic reason, support will feel robotic.
S1.notes.Q5: If I miss out on help because my group is treated differently, that's bad too, but unfairly flagging innocent people causes more harm than me missing a signal.
S1.notes.Q6: I already failed my last course in year one of the previous program. I don't need to be reminded once a year; if the model sees something wrong, it should tell me immediately.
S1.notes.Q7: A generic email is annoying and might trigger alarm for no reason. But with personalized emails referencing specific issues, sending to more people feels safer than risking a missed warning.

S2.notes.Q3: Using my own history helps: grades and program type are relevant but intrusive. Age is strictly confidential in Denmark (1978 law), so I'd never accept it. Disability data needs huge improvement to justify tracking, as it's about inclusion not exclusion.
S2.notes.Q4: Trust is everything here. Without an explanation, I won't click the link because it feels like surveillance. If they say 'we need your help,' that explains enough for me to care.
S2.notes.Q5: I am already from a disadvantaged background (non-EU student, working part-time). If the model misses my peers more often than others, it's discriminatory. I'd accept losing 3 cases to ensure we don't systematically overlook people like me.
S2.notes.Q6: I need support that feels real, not a generic mass email. A meeting invitation is scary but useful if I'm truly struggling. Generic emails are useless; phone calls are invasive.
S2.notes.Q7: If we can't get the right people, maybe it's better to miss some than call everyone every semester with generic advice.
S2.Q8.1: Students fear being labeled 'at risk' permanently before they know if it will actually help them recover rather than hinder their confidence.

S3.notes.Q3: Course grades help me understand my progress, so moderate improvement is okay. Admissions data (high school) feels like labeling someone before I start; only large improvements would justify it to avoid bias based on where I studied. Absalon activity (page views, late submissions) feels invasive and stressful for students with chronic health conditions who may not log in due to pain or fatigue—it creates anxiety rather than support.
S3.notes.Q4: I cannot imagine a 'no meaningful explanation' model for me as a student facing potential intervention; trust is essential here because I might receive personalized support based on an algorithm I don't understand. However, if there is even a small improvement in detection using moderate explainability, it becomes acceptable.
S3.notes.Q5: Making the model equally fair across groups is non-negotiable, but there must be a cost to accuracy. Losing up to 3-5 students identified overall seems manageable if it ensures marginalized peers are not systematically missed.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach (meeting or call) is much more acceptable than generic emails because my specific situation—health condition, reduced load—is relevant and reduces stigma compared to a 'system warning'. I prefer continuous monitoring but only if the threshold for triggering it feels like genuine concern.
S3.notes.Q7: "Fewer" is definitely not an option when personalized support is offered, as that risks missing me or others who could use help. For generic emails, a balance makes sense to avoid overwhelming students and waste of resources.
S3.Q8.1: The current credit-based rule ignores non-financial hardships like my health issues which affect attendance and grades differently than other students

S4.notes.Q3: Adding grades helps a lot since I fail sometimes, but my ADHD makes me lose focus too. Medium improvement is okay because it catches cases where the credit count alone misses my struggle.
S4.notes.Q4: High explainability (clear reasons) means advisors can build trust; small improvement justifies less transparency because we know where the system is coming from and why it flagged someone.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, knowing I'm 'first-gen' or if the system sees my financial aid status is crucial for context but still feels like invasive profiling unless there's a tangible help threshold.
S5.notes.Q4: The university already uses the credit rule (Very High). It is explainable and fairer than black-box AI, but I think even a clear reason like 'low grades' isn't enough when we have more data points. I want to know specifically why I'm flagged so I can address it.
S5.notes.Q5: The chart showing Group A having higher success rates makes me nervous; as a female student, I feel this bias often works against me in academia generally. Ensuring we catch everyone who needs help is more important than minimizing false positives that might just annoy students.
S5.notes.Q6: I'd prefer receiving an outreach at least twice per year as opposed to continuously being pestered about studies which feels like surveillance even if the intent is good support.
S5.notes.Q7: If it's a personalized email mentioning my specific situation, I'm okay with contacting more people to help them; but for general info (Generic Email), fewer students should be contacted.
S5.Q8.1: As an international student new here, the model needs to understand that 'struggling' might look different than struggling at home—I don't want my cultural context ignored in data patterns if they affect how I study or take exams.

S6.notes.Q3: Course grades help explain my situation as an international student, but Absalon data feels like surveillance; age is relevant for transition support.
S6.notes.Q4: Without a clear explanation, I won't trust the outreach or ask for help.
S6.notes.Q5: Missing students from my own background is worse than false positives; overall accuracy shouldn't suffer too much to fix this gap.
S6.notes.Q6: I need immediate contact; I once left university too late to get support when it was needed.
S6.notes.Q7: Personalized emails are better but still annoying; general info is a good starting point without stigma.
S6.Q8.1: Students might feel targeted and hidden from support due to language barriers or lack of confidence.

S7.notes.Q3: Course performance is basic but tracking page views feels like surveillance I don't want, especially since it predicts struggle before failure.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged so I can actually do something about it. A black box decision makes me defensive.
S7.notes.Q5: Missing people in marginalized groups is unfair, but getting false positives just to boost numbers feels useless and disrespectful.
S7.notes.Q6: Since I already know support exists for dyslexia, a proactive check-in could prevent me from burning out silently.
S7.notes.Q7: For personalized emails, I'd rather be sure it's relevant than having spammy outreach that feels like a hassle.

S8.notes.Q3: Course grades matter because I had bad grades and dropped out before, but age/gender are risky for discrimination since we are all equal citizens in Denmark.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to know WHY I was flagged so the advisor can talk about it, not just that a 'pattern' matched.
S8.notes.Q5: The goal is catching students in trouble like me, but we shouldn't miss anyone based on who they are; fairness means helping everyone equally to not repeat my failure.
S8.notes.Q6: Proactive support is best, but I'd prefer a personalized message over generic spam so it feels like genuine care.
S8.notes.Q7: A personal email might lead to false positives where students feel judged and stop contacting support, which is dangerous for vulnerable people.

S9.notes.Q3: I feel exposed about my disability, so I don't want data like that unless it helps me directly without surveillance vibes.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged so I can fix it or explain my situation, especially with mental health factors.
S9.notes.Q5: We shouldn't let groups like me get missed just to help others; fairness in catching students is crucial for equity.
S9.notes.Q6: I need constant support, not yearly checks, because my condition affects me irregularly throughout the semester.
S9.notes.Q7: , since a personalized message is already intrusive and should only go to those genuinely at risk with high confidence.
S9.Q8.1: Students might feel targeted or punished if the threshold isn't clear, making them avoid help-seeking even more.
